notice.title: History and imagination
notice.text: YUDDH is inspired by real history. Its battles, names and numbers are adapted to make a game, and some stories come from tradition rather than proof. Dates, battle sites, alliances and sequences of events are sometimes uncertain, debated, combined or invented for play, and where the game invents something it says so. Inscriptions and court chronicles show the view of the people who ordered them. Every battle has a History note with its sources, and each victory ends with a short epilogue.
notice.source: Tags: HISTORY (recorded in surviving sources), TRADITION (later stories, or readings historians debate), INVENTED (added by the game).

first_throne.happened: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya dynasty by displacing the Nandas of Magadha, conventionally dated around 322–321 BCE. How he did it is not securely known: the Greek and Roman writers say almost nothing about it, and the dramatic stories come from Indian texts written much later. The Nandas were remembered as rich and powerful; Plutarch repeats reports of a vast army with thousands of elephants, figures no historian trusts.

changed.text: The Nanda dynasty ended and Chandragupta's dynasty ruled Magadha. That change of power is the firm part of the story.
Chanakya (Kautilya) as Chandragupta's adviser comes from later Indian stories. Amatya Rakshasa and Parvataka are characters from the later play Mudrarakshasa, not proven participants.
One battle at the gates of Pataliputra. Its date, site and fighting are not recorded, and the seasons and every card's power are game rules.

first_throne.source: Sources: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 62; Justin 15.4; the Puranas and Buddhist and Jain traditions; Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa (a later drama); Jansari, Chandragupta Maurya (UCL Press).
first_throne.epilogue: Chandragupta held Pataliputra and went on to bring most of the north under one rule. A few years later he would meet the Greek-ruled lands at the Indus.

indus_line.happened: Around 305–303 BCE Seleucus I, one of Alexander's successors, crossed toward the Indus and dealt with Chandragupta until they made an agreement. Ancient writers record its terms: Seleucus gave up some eastern lands, the two courts were joined by a marriage arrangement, and Chandragupta sent 500 war elephants. Which lands, and who had the better of the fighting, nobody knows; no ancient writer shows either king as the clear winner.

changed.text: A treaty with territory, elephants and a marriage tie is recorded by Strabo, Justin and Appian, writing long after the event.
A battle on the Indus with a winner. The sources do not say where the armies met or how the fighting went.
The figure of 500 elephants is the ancient one, and round numbers may be exaggerated. The story of Seleucus's daughter Helena is a later popular addition.
Macedonian pikes (the phalanx), Companion cavalry and Cretan archers are how Hellenistic armies fought. Megasthenes was a Greek envoy at Pataliputra; his Indica survives only in fragments.

indus_line.source: Sources: Strabo 15.2.9; Justin 15.4; Appian, Syrian Wars 55; Plutarch; fragments of Megasthenes; Jansari, Chandragupta Maurya (UCL Press).
indus_line.epilogue: The treaty settled the frontier for a generation. Seleucus turned west, where tradition says his elephants served him at the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, and Chandragupta's empire held the north-west.

digvijaya.happened: The Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar carries a praise-poem for Samudragupta by his court poet Harishena. It names northern kings it says he "uprooted", among them Ganapatinaga, Nagasena and Achyutanandin, and twelve southern kings who were captured and then released and restored. Forest rulers, frontier kingdoms and distant powers are said to have paid tribute or sent envoys. His gold coins show him playing the veena.

changed.text: One battle at Padmavati against three Naga kings together. The pillar names the kings but gives no site, date or account of the fighting. Whether the Nagas fell once or twice is debated.
Poisoned arrows (Sarpa Vish). The cobra is the Naga symbol; the venom is the game's own idea.
The veena coin is real. The pillar is the winner's own account, so the defeated kings' side is missing.

digvijaya.source: Sources: Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar inscription by Harishena, as edited in Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum vol. III; Gupta lyrist gold coins (Indian Museum, Kolkata).
digvijaya.epilogue: After the north and the south, his gold coins proclaim an Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice of a sovereign. He did not rule everywhere directly: some kings were removed, some restored, and others only sent tribute and envoys. His son Chandragupta II would carry Gupta power west.

mahakantara.kicker: THE GREAT FOREST · mid-4th century CE
mahakantara.happened: The Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar names twelve southern kings that Samudragupta took captive and then released, restoring their kingdoms. Vyaghraraja of Mahakantara, "the Great Forest", is one of them. The Pillar also says the forest rulers (the Atavikas) were made servants of his service. Where Mahakantara lay is argued; the forest country of central India and Odisha is the usual guess.

changed.text: The battle. The Pillar names Vyaghraraja but gives no site, date or fight. Hidden archers, forest elephants and snares are the game's picture of a forest war.
The forest people are shown as an organised kingdom with its own stockades, not as primitives. The Pillar says only that they were subdued.
Capture, then release, is how the Pillar describes the southern kings. The card Grahana-Moksha is built on it.
Harishena, who composed the Pillar, serves in the game as a minister with the army; that he marched with it is the game's picture.

mahakantara.source: Sources: Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar inscription by Harishena, as edited in Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum vol. III.
mahakantara.epilogue: Vyaghraraja was set free and his forest country given back to him, as the Pillar says of all twelve. The Gupta column turned toward the eastern coast and the south.

kanchi.kicker: THE WALLS OF KANCHI · mid-4th century CE
kanchi.happened: Vishnugopa of Kanchi is the seventh of the twelve southern kings named on the Prayaga Pillar, which says he was captured and released like the rest. Kanchi (Kanchipuram) was a Pallava city on the south-east coast, the far end of the Pillar's list. How far south Samudragupta's march really went is debated.

changed.text: The siege, the walls and the fight. The Pillar gives no account of any battle at Kanchi, and says nothing of Gupta rule being set up there.
Which Pallava ruler Vishnugopa was is debated. Kanchi's Ghatika college is known from later inscriptions; the game lets the city be a place of scholars already, its own licence.
Capture and release is the Pillar's claim. It is the victor's own record, so Kanchi's side of the story is missing.

kanchi.source: Sources: Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar inscription by Harishena, as edited in Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum vol. III.
kanchi.epilogue: Vishnugopa was released and restored. Kanchi stayed Pallava for centuries; its kings would one day capture Badami, the Chalukya capital.

tarain1.kicker: THE FIRST BATTLE OF TARAIN · 1191 CE
tarain1.happened: In the winter of 1190-91 Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghor, ruler of Ghur and Ghazni, took the fortress of Tabarhinda (Bathinda) and left a garrison in it. Prithviraj III of the Chahamana (Chauhan) dynasty, lord of Ajmer and Delhi, marched against him with his feudatories and met the Ghurid army at Tarain (Taraori, Haryana). The Persian chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj, writing in 1260, says the Ghurid army was beaten. He tells how the sultan charged Govind Rai of Delhi, broke his teeth with a lance and was wounded in the arm by his javelin, and was led from the field by a young soldier. The sultan withdrew to Ghazni. In 1192 he came back and won the second battle of Tarain.

changed.text: The battle itself: the formations, the elephants and the drums. The sources give the outcome and a few moments, not the fight. There are no troop numbers because the large figures in later retellings are not trustworthy. The game plays it in its firm-ground season; the real battle was fought in the winter of early 1191.

Govindaraja is Minhaj's Govind Rai of Delhi, and the lance-and-javelin duel is his story. The Ghurid side is shown as the disciplined professional army it was, with drilled horse guards, mounted archers and kettle-drums.

Later Persian writers call Govind Rai Prithviraj's brother; Minhaj calls him the ruler of Delhi. Later accounts also differ on what happened at Tabarhinda: whether Prithviraj took the fort back or the garrison held out until the sultan returned. The game does not decide it.

tarain1.source: Sources: Minhaj-i Siraj, Tabaqat-i Nasiri (1260); Cynthia Talbot, The Last Hindu Emperor (2015), on the sources and the later legend; the Sanskrit Prithvirajavijaya for the Chahamana court's own voice. The late Prithviraj Raso is not used as evidence.
tarain1.epilogue: It was a clear victory and it settled nothing. The sultan went home, rebuilt his army and came back the next year.

tarain2.kicker: THE SECOND BATTLE OF TARAIN · 1192 CE
tarain2.happened: In 1192 Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghor returned to Tarain with a rebuilt army. The Persian chroniclers Minhaj-i Siraj and Hasan Nizami say the Ghurid army harassed the Rajput line with mounted archers, drew it out, and sent its heavy cavalry against it only when it was worn. The Rajput host broke. Prithviraj III was captured; the sources differ on how and when he died. Within a year or two Delhi and Ajmer came under Ghurid control, and the sultan's general Qutb al-Din Aibak stayed in India as his governor. The Delhi Sultanate grew from that base.

changed.text: The player commands the Rajputs and can win. In 1192 they lost. The battle itself, the card effects and the reserve's timing are the game's; there are no troop numbers because the large figures in later retellings are not trustworthy.

The Ghurid plan is the one the Persian chroniclers describe: harass with mounted archers, avoid a head-on clash, keep the heavy horse back, then strike. That is why Feigned Flight hurts a whole front line and the Mailed Reserve is expensive.

Later accounts name captains and tell of poets and legends around Prithviraj's fall (the blinding, the arrow, the poet Chand Bardai). They come from late sources and are not used as evidence. The name Skandaraja and the Charan bard are the game's figures for the Chahamana court and army, not claims about individuals.

tarain2.source: Sources: Minhaj-i Siraj, Tabaqat-i Nasiri (1260); Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir (early 13th c.); Cynthia Talbot, The Last Hindu Emperor (2015), on the sources and the later legend. The late Prithviraj Raso is not used as evidence.
tarain2.epilogue: The sources say the host broke in 1192 and the plain changed hands. Whatever you did here, the next chapter belongs to the governors who stayed behind.

lanka.kicker: THE CROSSING TO LANKA · c. 993 CE
lanka.happened: In about 993 CE a Chola army sent by Rajaraja I crossed the Palk Strait and took Anuradhapura, the ancient capital of northern Sri Lanka. The island's chronicle, the Culavamsa, says King Mahinda V had already lost his hold: his unpaid army would not obey him, and he withdrew south to Ruhuna. Chola inscriptions call the conquered north Ila-mandalam, and the port of Mahatittha was renamed Rajarajapura. Rajendra I completed the conquest of the island around 1017 and Mahinda V was taken to India. Chola rule there ended in 1070 under Vijayabahu I.

changed.text: The battle itself: the beach, the elephants and the fight at the reservoir. The sources say the north was taken, not how.

Both voices are kept: the Chola record says it was conquered, the chronicle says the king's own army had stopped obeying him. Neither is a neutral witness. The game cannot start the Sinhalese side with an empty treasury, so it gives them fewer ways to pay for war instead.

Scholars differ on how much of the island fell in 993 and how much in the later campaigns. Vandiyadevan is a name from Chola tradition for a commander of Rajaraja's time; his part in the crossing is the game's licence.

lanka.source: Sources: the Culavamsa (the Sinhalese chronicle); Chola inscriptions of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I (South Indian Inscriptions); K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas; Sri Lankan histories of the Anuradhapura–Polonnaruva transition.
lanka.epilogue: The Cholas held the north for about eighty years. Rajaraja's son would finish the island, and Anuradhapura, the capital for over a thousand years, never again became the seat of a Sinhalese king.

ganga.happened: Rajendra I's inscriptions say a Chola army marched north from the Godavari through Kalinga and Odisha into Bengal, beat several kings on the way and then Mahipala I of the Pala empire, and carried Ganga water back south. Rajendra did not lead it: the general Araiyan Rajarajan did, and the emperor waited on the Godavari and met the army on its return. He then founded a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram ("the city of the Chola who took the Ganga"), with a great tank his record calls a "liquid pillar of victory".

changed.text: The battle itself: the river line, the elephants and the boats. The inscription names the kings beaten, not how they were beaten.

Mahipala's Buddhist monasteries are real, and the Palas were patrons of Bihar and Bengal's great vihara schools; the game gives him a teacher card as a nod to that. The size of the armies is not known.
Many popular accounts say Rajendra marched to the Ganga himself. His own inscriptions give the march to his general. The game follows the inscriptions.

ganga.source: Sources: Rajendra I's Tamil prasasti and the Tiruvalangadu plates; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas; summaries of the Chola expedition to the Ganges in standard histories.
ganga.epilogue: The Cholas did not keep Bengal. The army went home with the water, the tribute and the prestige, and the Palas ruled on. What stayed behind was a new capital in the south named for the river.

kadaram.happened: Rajendra I (ruled about 1014–1044), son of Rajaraja, sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal in about 1025. His own Tamil inscriptions, from about his fourteenth regnal year (c. 1026), list the cities taken: Kadaram (usually identified with Kedah on the Malay coast), Srivijaya itself and other ports, and say its king, Sangrama Vijayottungavarman, was captured. Why is argued: Chola merchant guilds traded across the Bay, and a quarrel over trade, a show of prestige and a wish to open the sea routes have all been suggested.

changed.text: The battle itself: the boat wall, the fire boats and the fight in the harbour. The inscriptions list what was taken, not how.

The identification of Kadaram with Kedah, and the size of the Chola fleet, are scholars' readings of sparse evidence. The game gives the Ainnurruvar guild an armed guard; the guild's part in the venture is its own licence.

Our old prototype set this under Rajaraja in 1014. The Kadaram expedition belongs to his son Rajendra, c. 1025. Srivijaya's own side is hardly recorded, so the game paints it as a rich, dignified trading realm, not a nest of pirates.

kadaram.source: Sources: Rajendra I's Tamil prasasti of his 14th regnal year (South Indian Inscriptions); Kenneth Hall, Maritime Trade and State Development in Early Southeast Asia; Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas.
kadaram.epilogue: The inscriptions record no lasting Chola rule overseas. Within a few years Srivijaya's ports traded again, and the Cholas went back to the Ganga and the Deccan: a raid of prestige and trade, not a conquest.

golden_age.happened: Chandragupta II (ruled about 375–415 CE) ended the rule of the Western Kshatrapas, Saka kings who had ruled Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra for centuries. A cave inscription at Udayagiri, dated about 401 CE, records his minister travelling with the king as he sought to conquer the whole earth. The Kshatrapa silver coins stop, and Gupta silver coins in the same style appear, around 409 CE. When and where the last fighting happened is not recorded.

changed.text: One battle at Ujjain against Rudrasimha III, and his fall in it. The coins show a change of rule, not a battle. The game labels the war "c. 400 CE" to fit the Udayagiri date; the silver coins are about 409.
Vikramaditya and the nine gems (Navaratna), with the poet Kalidasa among them, are a later legend. Historians debate who Vikramaditya was.
The Iron Pillar of Delhi is often linked to Chandragupta II, but its king is only named "Chandra", and nothing says it defended Ujjain.
The desert storm (Marubhumi Toofan) is the game's own.

golden_age.source: Sources: Udayagiri cave inscriptions (Gupta year 82, about 401 CE); Western Kshatrapa and Gupta silver coins; later Sanskrit tradition of Vikramaditya; Delhi Iron Pillar inscription.
golden_age.epilogue: With the west won, Gupta rule reached the Arabian Sea and its trading ports, and its coins carried a new image in a familiar silver style. The Chinese monk Faxian travelled through the empire around these years.

narmada_line.happened: Harsha of Kanauj (reigned 606–647 CE) was the strongest ruler of the north. At some point before 634 CE he marched south against Pulakeshin II of Badami and was stopped at the Narmada. The Chalukya poet Ravikirti recorded it in the Aihole inscription of 634–635 CE, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who knew Harsha's court, also describes Harsha's failure in the south. The river stayed the border between the two empires.

changed.text: The clash, and the Chalukya claim of success, are recorded. The Aihole inscription is a praise-poem written by the winner's poet.
The ford, the armies, the turns of the fight and the date. Nobody knows where or when it happened, and dates from c. 612 to c. 630 CE are argued.
Harsha is shown as an emperor of wide reach, a poet and a giver: Bana's biography and Xuanzang describe his five-yearly giving at Prayaga.

narmada_line.source: Sources: Aihole inscription of Ravikirti (634–635 CE); Bana, Harshacharita; Xuanzang, Records of the Western World.
narmada_line.epilogue: Pulakeshin II took the title Parameshvara and ruled a Deccan empire from the Narmada to the Kaveri. Harsha never marched south again; he died in 647 CE and his empire broke apart within a generation. In 642 CE the Pallava king Narasimhavarman captured Badami.
